newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS - Texas Instruments calls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS - Texas Instruments calls.

text.p: Activity in Texas Instruments Inc options was hectic as the stock spiked up on news of a $1 billion royalty deal with Samsung Electronics Co Ltd, traders said.
Texas Instruments stock was up 4-1/2 to 61 in late trade and had triggered good volume in December and January 60 call options.

The rally pushed the stock above the 55 and 60 strike prices, where a lot of option open interest had accumulated to form resistance levels, said Todd Salamone, senior research analyst at Cincinnati-based Investment Research Institute.
"Technicals are shaping up bullishly...fundamentals are looking better, and from an options perspective it looks pretty good," Salamone said.
December and January calls on the Chicago Board Options Exchange had turnover of 4,094 and 3,928 contracts respectively by late trade.
The January 60 had fairly substantial open interest of 7,581 contracts as of end-Monday.
The stock had previously peaked in the 60 area in April and October, Salamone added.
He cautioned that the market was thin and choppy today due to the Thanksgiving Day holiday Thursday and that he wanted to see the stock settle above the 60 level next week to be really bullish.
Earlier in the day, the stock jumped on news that Texas Instruments had reached an agreement with Samsung on a 10-year cross-licensing deal that could result in more than $1 billion in royalties.
"It's driven by news, basically," said Rod Jamieson, vice president of options strategy at EVEREN Securities.
He added that trading could stay volatile for the rest of the week because bidders or sellers could suddenly evaporate.
"There have been a few more air pockets today than there have been in the past (several days)," he said.
Chris Bookmyer, a CBOE designated primary market maker with TradeNet, said the technology sector was likely to remain the center of the market's volatility.

She noted that the broad market opened strong, boosted partly by Texas Instruments news, and then pulled back on bearishness in some other high tech names, reflecting traders' nervousness particularly in the high-tech sector.
Jamieson agreed that technology stocks were becoming increasingly high-risk issues, whether they were traded from the bearish side or the bullish side.

"They're all holding up pretty well, considering how much run they've had," he said. "I would expect that at some point they're going to have a retest and sell off, but trying to pick that point is like standing in front of a freight train."
